text: Everything in this chapter — hypervisors, vCPUs, virtual memory, virtual disks — isn't background theory. It's literally what a public cloud provider's datacenter is. Behind every AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region are rows of physical servers, each running a Type 1 hypervisor, each hosting dozens or hundreds of customer virtual machines. When you launch an EC2 instance, you're not getting new hardware — you're getting a VM carved out of a server that was already running.

AWS's own hypervisor platform is called Nitro, a lightweight KVM-based hypervisor combined with dedicated Nitro Cards that offload networking, storage, and security away from the main CPU, so nearly all the server's compute goes to customer VMs. Microsoft Azure runs its compute fleet on a heavily customized, hardened version of Hyper-V, the same Type 1 hypervisor from Lesson 19, scaled for multi-tenant cloud use.

That's why launching a cloud VM takes seconds, not hours. An API call to launch an instance really just tells an already-running hypervisor on an already-running physical host to start a new VM from a template image, with a given amount of vCPU and RAM. That's a software operation the hypervisor finishes in seconds — no racking, no cabling, no installing an OS from scratch.

Running VMs from different customers on the very same physical server is called multi-tenancy, and it only works because the hypervisor enforces strict isolation between every VM, using the same vCPU scheduling and memory mapping boundaries from earlier in this chapter. Your VM cannot see or touch another customer's memory, disk, or network traffic, even on the exact same physical box.

That draws a hard physical line between the provider and the customer: the provider owns, patches, and secures the hypervisor and the physical hardware underneath it, and the customer owns everything from the guest OS up — patching the VM, configuring applications, securing data.
That line is the shared responsibility model, and it's exactly where Chapter 6 picks up, starting with the cloud service models — IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS — in the very next lesson.
